title: Better awareness of potential key worker shortages ought to increase public support for universities
summary: Higher education finances are all over the papers – but the potential effect on local key worker pipelines is not. For Steve Briggs, it’s incumbent on the sector to get this message across
full_text:
Civic mission renewal is currently a strategic priority for universities in the UK. A key driver for this work has been a recognition that universities need to re-establish relevance and build public trust and backing.

To secure increased public support, universities are seeking to explicitly demonstrate to local communities how they directly improve the prospects and living standards of those living immediately within their constituency.

Rethinking communication with local stakeholders is evidently going to be critical to civic renewal. To restore local support, universities need high impact and clear messages that resonate with their communities. Such messages must work for all, regardless of political affiliation.

I propose that one such message could involve a coordinated sector effort to evidence the critical contributions that universities make to training key workers across their respective regions. This would include nurses, midwives, allied health professionals (such as paramedics and radiographers), doctors, surgeons, teachers and social workers. Along with engineers who design and manage transport, energy and utility infrastructures. Associated messaging could highlight key worker successes, such as graduate outcomes statistics (including how many stay local to work) and alumni profiles.

A time bomb hidden in plain sight

The unprecedented financial distress being experienced by the UK higher education sector has been widely reported. To date, efforts to make savings have largely been left to individual institutions to decide rather than coordinated centrally. Left unchecked, this creates a possibility of higher education cold spots’emerging erratically and possibly with very limited warning.

This presents an existential risk to key worker training systems and significantly undermines the ability to plan for the long-term. Local community awareness of potential future disruption to keyworker pipelines would directly impact support for their local university. However, this issue does not even seem to be on the radar of mass media channels.

Let’s consider nursing as an example. There is already a major recruitment crisis for nurses the UK. The Royal College of Nursing has pointed out that there are currently 29,000 registered nursing vacancies in the NHS alone. This can be attributed to multiple factors including employment conditions (such as working hours, pay concerns and job pressures), an ageing workforce and capacity to train new starters. To address this, it is imperative to develop a long-term plan related to increasing training and recruitment of nurses across the UK.

There are approximately 90 UK universities that offer courses and UCAS reported that in 2025, there were 26,315 applicants accepted on to corresponding courses. Given than 4 out of 10 universities reported a deficit in 2025–26 it is reasonable to anticipate that multiple institutions delivering nursing courses are experiencing financial challenges.

The loss of any provider would be damaging in terms of nurse numbers – and in the case of multiple providers, potentially catastrophic.

Furthermore, there are regions in the UK where a reduction in providers would be felt even more heavily. For instance, in rural parts of the UK there are single universities which serve large catchment areas. For example, the Southwest Peninsula (Devon/Cornwall), the North West (Cumbria) and the East of England (Norfolk / Suffolk). Accordingly, any disruption to corresponding nursing training pathways would be far reaching.

Equally, disruption in an urban region where there are multiple universities could be similarly damaging. For instance, in London there are over 30 universities of which around 20 teach nursing. However, there are over 80 NHS hospitals and therefore are significant nurse turnover and recruitment demands that need to be serviced.

Time for honest conversation

Few in the UK would argue with the need to sustain (and potentially expand) the number of key workers. Hence, regardless of whatever an individual considers to be the “optimum” number of universities in the UK, a continued need for regional key worker training facilities is hard to debate.

It is therefore critical that there are pre-emptive and transparent conversations regarding the extent to which existing key worker training could be negatively impacted by future changes to universities. Equally, there should be widely accessible public information around the extent to which safeguarding and mitigation for key worker training would be possible in the event of multiple universities downsizing or even leaving the market.

It is my view that sharing such implications with the public now may have a fundamental impact on how higher education contraction is perceived and associated action that is expected from the government. Providing answers to such questions after the event is going to be too late. Given the absence of mass media coverage related to these risks, I suggest that there is an imperative for universities themselves to spell this out.

title: Rethinking the price and value of a degree in a changing world

The post Rethinking the price and value of a degree in a changing world appeared first on HEPI.
full_text:
This blog was kindly authored by Professor Deba Bardhan Correia, Dean – Faculty of Business, Humanities & Social Sciences, and Chris Payne, Registrar & Chief Administrative Officer, both of the University of Buckingham.

We are at a point where the question is no longer simply what higher education costs, but whether students perceive it to be worth it at all.

As Buckingham marks its 50th anniversary, this provides an opportunity to reflect on how the higher education landscape is changing and how, in many respects, it remains the same.

The Lifelong Learning Entitlement, the emergence of artificial intelligence and changing attitudes towards education are beginning to reshape how learning is perceived, accessed and consumed. Yet the fee structure for full undergraduate degrees has remained remarkably stable regardless of subject demand, subject nature or the mode and cost of delivery. In contrast, graduate outcomes are more variable, student satisfaction is under greater scrutiny and the cost-of-living crisis has intensified questions about what a university education is worth and whether the traditional model continues to meet student expectations.

What has changed most significantly is the context in which students make decisions. University is no longer compared solely with other universities. Increasingly, prospective students weigh higher education against degree apprenticeships, employment, entrepreneurship and more flexible forms of learning. They are considering opportunity costs alongside tuition fees and asking what they will gain, how long it will take and whether there are different routes to achieve similar outcomes.

At the same time, artificial intelligence is reshaping assumptions about skills, careers and the future of work. For many students, the question is no longer simply whether they can afford university, but whether a degree represents the right investment of time, money and effort in an increasingly uncertain environment.

Alongside these developments, student expectations are changing. Concerns around mental health are more visible, and a growing number of students are choosing to remain at home and commute rather than move away. Cost is one factor, but so too are support networks, wellbeing and individual learning needs. Greater awareness of neurodiversity has also highlighted that students engage with learning in different ways and thrive in different environments. These factors add further nuance to how students assess both the value and the risks associated with attending university.

Risk, in fact, is becoming an increasingly important part of the conversation.

Prospective students rarely make decisions based on detailed modelling of long-term student loan repayments. Instead, they make judgements based on the headline cost, the length of study, employment prospects and the alternatives available to them. The challenge for universities is therefore not simply affordability. It is helping students navigate uncertainty.

These decisions are being made in a changed environment as well. Whilst the previous generations often relied on schools, universities and family networks to understand the value of higher education, today’s applicants encounter a constant stream of peer-generated content across TikTok, Instagram, YouTube, Reddit and LinkedIn, where higher education is discussed, debated and scrutinised in real time.

The significance of social media is not that it changes the facts about higher education, but that it changes how those facts are interpreted. A graduate discussing difficulties finding work after completing a degree, an apprentice sharing earnings progression, or a young entrepreneur explaining why they bypassed university altogether can influence perceptions far beyond their own experience.

Consider the influence of TikTok. A video entitled “Why I regret my degree” or “Why I chose a degree apprenticeship instead of university” can reach hundreds of thousands of viewers within days. Equally, content documenting accommodation costs, graduate job searches or alternative career pathways often generates extensive engagement. Such experiences may not be representative, but they are frequently perceived as authentic and relatable.

For Generation Z, value is no longer defined solely by institutions. It is increasingly negotiated through networks of peers, creators and online communities. Higher education therefore operates not only in a marketplace of educational choices but also in a marketplace of narratives where what students hear from others can be as influential as what universities say about themselves.

Lower tuition fees and shorter degrees can help address some of these concerns. They reduce the amount students need to borrow and lower wider costs associated with study, including accommodation and living expenses. While this may not significantly change eventual repayment patterns for every graduate, it can alter perceptions of risk at the point of entry. In that sense, the effect is as much psychological as financial.

Sometimes a relatively modest difference in cost or duration may be the factor that enables a student to choose higher education rather than walk away from it altogether.

The labour market those students seek to enter is itself changing. Artificial intelligence is beginning to reshape entry-level work in many sectors. At the same time, some graduates report applying for large numbers of positions without success and, even when employment is secured, it is not always aligned with the level or subject of study. These realities inevitably influence how prospective students evaluate the financial and non-financial returns of higher education.

The University of Buckingham’s decision to reduce tuition fees on selected programmes to £7,830, (the lower limit accessible through Student Finance England), was therefore a deliberate one. As an independent university, we have greater flexibility to ask questions about pricing, provision and student demand that may be more difficult elsewhere. We are seeking to test broad proposition: that high-quality higher education can be delivered at this price point and that lower costs may encourage students who are questioning the value of a degree to reconsider their options. Lowering the headline price, alongside offering a shorter and more intensive degree, speaks directly to the factors students tell us matter most: cost, time and perceived value.

The courses included within the initiative are concentrated in areas where demand remains strong, including business and creative writing. This reflects how students are making increasingly sophisticated judgements about future opportunities and are often gravitating towards subjects they believe will provide versatility in a changing labour market.

Taken together, these developments suggest a different way of thinking about higher education provision. Students are not simply comparing repayment profiles. They are making broader assessments about risk, flexibility, experience and return. The question is not whether a degree has value, but how that value is understood, communicated and experienced by different groups of students.

The wider challenge for the sector is whether current structures reflect these realities with sufficient nuance. A largely uniform fee structure sits uneasily alongside a student population whose needs, expectations and constraints are becoming increasingly diverse.

As students make decisions about their futures, universities should recognise that they are not rejecting higher education. Rather, they are becoming more discerning consumers of it and increasingly, they are asking questions collectively in digital spaces where perceptions are formed socially and shared rapidly.

If students are asking whether university is worth it, the response cannot be reassurance alone. We must provide greater transparency about costs, experiences and outcomes, alongside a recognition that there is no longer a single student journey. In the years ahead, universities that thrive are likely to be those most willing to engage honestly with this complexity, rather than assuming yesterday’s answers will continue to satisfy tomorrow’s students.

title: Student bank accounts: don’t be swayed by the freebies, freshers told
summary:
Sign-up perks may capture the attention but should the focus be on the interest-free overdraft?

  • The best student deals and discounts

full_text:
In the scramble to sort out university accommodation, join freshers group chats and work out how a student loan payment is meant to stretch across a whole term, there is one big decision that is easy to put off but worth getting right: which student bank account to open.

Student accounts work like any other current account but come with two extras that don’t apply to the general public: an interest-free overdraft, and a lot of perks designed to hook you in as a customer for life.

However, while it is tempting to choose an account on the strength of the free cash, vouchers or other goodies, personal finance experts advise you not to be swayed by the extras.

“An interest-free overdraft could provide greater value over the course of a degree than a one-off freebie,” says Caitlyn Eastell at Moneyfactscompare.co.uk.

The ranking of the best student bank accounts for 2026-27 by the website Save the Student also places an emphasis on the size of the interest-free overdraft. “Maintenance loans now fall short of living costs by an average of £502 per month,” says Tom Allingham, the site’s student banking expert.

Its top picks for this year are the NatWest/Royal Bank of Scotland (RBS) student account, Nationwide FlexStudent and the Santander Edge student account.

To help you make your own mind up, here’s what’s on offer.

Santander Edge student current account

Freebies: a free four-year 16-25 Railcard, which is good for a third off most rail fares in Great Britain, as well as discounts on the tube when linked to an Oyster card. For students who travel home regularly, it is one of the more valuable perks on the market, potentially saving hundreds of pounds a year.

Interest-free overdraft: £1,500 in years one to three, but up to £2,000 in year five (if relevant).

Anything else? A prize draw: everyone who opens an account between 14 July and 16 October and makes a debit card purchase by the end of December is guaranteed at least £20, with one lucky student walking away with £100,000. Further prizes of £10,000, £1,000 and £100 are also on offer.

NatWest/RBS student account

Freebies: £100 cash, plus a four-year Tastecard subscription, which gets you money off at thousands of restaurants and cafes across the UK. NatWest says the Tastecard is worth £79.99 a year, although at the time of writing it was on sale for £39.99.

Interest-free overdraft: up to £2,000 from the second term of the first year (up to £500 available from day one), rising to up to £3,250 from year three onwards – one of the largest on the market.

Anything else? RBS is running an identical offer to NatWest for students in Scotland.

Nationwide FlexStudent

Freebies: £100 cash plus £120 in Just Eat vouchers, paid as £10 a month for a year. To unlock the offer, students need to pay in £500 and make five debit card payments by 11 December.

Interest-free overdraft: up to £1,000 in year one, up to £2,000 in year two and up to £3,000 in year three. (Your limit stays at £3,000 if your course is longer.)

Anything else? You could get a “Fairer Share” payment: each year since 2023, Nationwide has paid £100 to eligible members with a qualifying current account and savings or mortgage. Also, there are no fees for using the debit card abroad.

Lloyds/Bank of Scotland student account

Freebies: £100 to anyone who opens (or switches to) the account and pays in at least £500 by 30 October, plus up to £120 in Deliveroo vouchers – paid as £20 a month for six months to those making 20 or more debit card payments each month between November and April.

Interest-free overdraft: up to £1,500 in years one to three, rising to £2,000 for those studying on courses of four years or more.

Anything else? Both let you earn up to 15% cashback on everyday spending with selected retailers. Lloyds is also offering a prize draw in which five students will each win £9,790 – equivalent of a year’s maximum tuition fees in England.

HSBC Student bank account

Freebies: none at the time of writing.

Interest-free overdraft: up to £1,000 from day one, then up to £2,000 in year two, and up to £3,000 in year three.

Anything else? Access to HSBC’s 5% regular saver account, and to discounts via its home&Away offers programme.

Barclays Student Additions account

Freebies: none at the time of writing.

Interest-free overdraft: up to £500 from day one, rising to £1,000 in year one, and then up to £1,500 in year two and beyond.

Anything else? Not much to shout about this year.

TSB student bank account

Freebies: none at the time of writing, but the account pays a generous 5% (variable) interest on balances up to £500 – worth up to £25 a year.

Interest-free overdraft: up to £500 during the first six months, then up to £1,000 from months seven to nine, then up to £1,500 from month 10 onwards.

Anything else? Nothing of note.

Whichever account you choose, remember that the overdraft is not free money forever: once you graduate, most accounts convert into a graduate account that gradually withdraws the interest-free borrowing over a year or two, after which unpaid balances start accruing interest like any other loan.

title: Under UT’s New Core Curriculum, Humanities Benefit but Faculty Are Limited
summary:
Under UT’s New Core Curriculum, Humanities Benefit but Faculty Are Limited
Emma Whitford Tue, 08/18/2026 - 03:00 AM

The new core will include a list of approved authors that faculty must select from to build their syllabi for certain courses, including Great Questions of Human Life and Masterworks of Literature.

Byline(s)
Emma Whitford
full_text:
The University of Texas at Austin unveiled its new core curriculum last week, 10 months after President Jim Davis instructed a faculty task force to review the existing general education requirements and “identify gaps in quality, rigor, or intellectual cohesion.” The resulting proposal was presented on Thursday to the University of Texas System Board of Regents, whose members applauded the committee for their work and embraced the new plan; one board member, Stuart Stedman, said he got “misty-eyed” reading the task force’s report.

The new core splits requirements into three pillars—arts and humanities, social sciences, and STEM—which represent the “three main spheres of intellectual endeavor,” the report states. For all core classes, it says, the university should prioritize small class sizes and writing assignments and minimize online teaching. In total, students will have to take 36 general education credits, down from 42. The STEM requirements are watered down while the humanities receive greater attention, faculty members told Inside Higher Ed.

For some requirements, such as U.S. History or Foundations of Social Science, faculty will suggest existing or new courses that could satisfy the requirement. Other requirements, like Great Questions of Human Life and Great Ideas in Science, will likely have classes built specifically around them. The proposed core also includes a Western civilization credit that replaces one of two currently required U.S. history courses, and a computer science and artificial intelligence requirement. A world politics and culture requirement was added to balance the Western civilization requirement, said Devin Stauffer, a government professor and chair of the task force.

Inside Higher Ed spoke with seven faculty members about the new core, and it received mixed reviews. Some professors said they appreciated seeing general education requirements take center stage. “In higher education, we have to get very used to the fact that we’re preparing our students for change that we can’t predict, and the core curriculum is where that conversation happens,” said chemistry professor Brent Iverson. Other faculty members expressed concern that the proposal takes a Western-centric approach to the general education curriculum. Still others said that the process of developing the new core was not transparent and reflects a top-down approach that doesn’t value faculty expertise.

The task force worked against a tumultuous political backdrop. Texas Senate Bill 37—which dictates that all public institutions in the state review their general education curricula every five years—was enacted a month before the task force was formed. After the law took effect, other Texas public systems, including Texas A&M and Texas Tech, implemented strict rules about how faculty could speak and teach about gender, sexuality and race. Nearly every four-year public institution undertook a comprehensive syllabi review, and faculty at several public universities were punished for their political speech.

But politics didn’t come up often in their work, Stauffer told Inside Higher Ed. “Politically speaking, there was a range of views on the committee, but we actually didn’t get into political arguments. It was in the backdrop, but it wasn’t really front and center in our conversations,” he said.

Other faculty are skeptical, however, that politics didn’t influence the resulting curriculum. Many of the faculty on the 22-member appointed task force “were selected for their conservative viewpoints,” said Julie Minich, a literature professor who previously taught American literature for the core. (That class is now being repackaged as Masterworks of American Literature.)

“I am quite shocked at the fact that they have not sought any faculty input except for people handpicked by the president,” Minich said. “There’s not any kind of mechanism for people who’ve actually been teaching these classes … to give any kind of feedback.”

Lauren Gutterman, an associate professor of American studies and vice president of the American Association of University Professors chapter at UT Austin, shared similar thoughts.

“The new Western civilization requirement, I think, clearly reflects [Provost William Inboden’s] views and is a direct response to what right-wing think tanks like the Heritage Foundation and the Manhattan Institute have been calling for in terms of transformation of higher education,” she said.

Courses approved to satisfy the requirement “will focus on capacious themes, great ideas, and broad historical developments, such as the Renaissance, the Reformation, and the Enlightenment, the rise of modern science and industry, or the development of liberal democratic nation-states,” the task force’s report states.

“The provost office left it in our hands,” Stauffer said. “And we had a wide range of opinions and some really good discussions among the group. I think the group was a more broad, more diverse group than some people on campus may think it is.”

During deliberations, “the argument was made that [the proposed core] is a little too West-centric. So we said, ‘OK, let’s have a world politics and cultures piece of this as well,’” he continued. “I understand where that critique [that the curriculum is too focused on the West] is coming from, but we were mindful of that and tried to address it. Our addressing of it may not be to everyone’s satisfaction, but it wasn’t something we ignored or didn’t care about.”

‘Not Killing Those Classes Yet’

Several proposed courses—such as Great Questions of Human Life and Masterworks of Literature—will require that at least two-thirds of assigned texts are pulled from curated lists of 40 approved authors. The purpose of the lists is to “create something of a common experience for the students,” Stauffer said. The number 40 was his idea—a play on UT’s nickname of “the Forty Acres”—but he expects more authors will eventually be included. It is yet to be determined who will decide which authors make the cut.

Faculty find the lists limiting, several told Inside Higher Ed. They also worry they won’t include enough women and nonwhite authors.

“We have to ask who’s probably not going to be on that list of 40 thinkers and writers, and I think it’s going to be a lot of women writers, a lot of authors of color,” said Gretchen Murphy, an English professor at UT.

Over all, however, she believes the English department’s prior contributions to the core were largely retained in the new model. “Humanities is the winner,” she said. Stauffer also said the task force was focused on giving humanities a larger part in the core.

Several faculty members shared concerns that moving certain classes outside the core will weaken already-vulnerable departments, including the now-consolidated ethnic studies and women’s and gender studies departments. During Thursday’s board meeting, board chairman Kevin Eltife repeatedly emphasized that elective classes will be evaluated by enrollments.

“Take something out of the core, and make it elective, it’s going to have to stand on its own in terms of supply and demand. So that course, whatever it is, may have had 200 students because it was a core course. If it becomes an elective, there might be only three people enrolled,” he said. “You’re not killing those classes yet, but the supply and demand is going to determine the catalog at some point.”

In the proposed core’s third pillar, STEM, students will take 12 credits. According to physics professor Peter Onyisi, the proposal “significantly weakens” the STEM portion of general education at UT. He takes particular issue with the Great Ideas in Science class, which aims to “help students appreciate the beauty of science as well as its explanatory power,” according to the report. He likened it to “episodes of NOVA with homework.”

“It really comes across as a class that’s intended to make people think, ‘Ah, science is great,’” Onyisi said. “I was joking with people that it should probably be called Bad Ideas in Science, because … most of science is not landmark breakthroughs. Most of science is hunting to figure out how to explain something you don’t quite understand or your experiment doesn’t quite work. Filtering science through very specific breakthroughs is really discarding most of what science is, and I think is doing students a disservice to present science in that way.”

He also believes the artificial intelligence requirement “is almost certainly going to be outmoded the moment it’s taught,” he said.

The proposed curriculum has not been approved by the Texas Higher Education Coordinating Board, which is required for all general education curricula in Texas. But that process will be a bit more complicated this year, because while UT revamps its core, the coordinating board is also revising its standards. It may be a couple of years before it’s clear how UT’s plan aligns with state requirements, Stauffer said.

“We’ve moved before they moved,” he said. “They have a process of coming up with a new set of core requirements, but we went ahead and just did what we thought was best first, and we’re hoping that what we came up with will be regarded by the Higher Education Coordinating Board as compliant with their new framework.”

title: Report: Benchmarking Online Ed
summary:
Report: Benchmarking Online Ed
colleen.flaherty Tue, 08/18/2026 - 03:00 AM
Byline(s)
Colleen Flaherty
full_text:
Last year, the online and professional education association UPCEA urged institutions to close the gap between student expectations on institutional preparedness for online learning as part of its annual report on the Benchmarking Online Enterprises Survey. This year’s report, released Monday, warns that the story beneath the 2026 data isn’t one of a “rising tide lifting every online enterprise equally, but rather a sector beginning to sort itself into those pulling ahead and those bracing for contraction.”

The average online enterprise budget increased from $8.1 million in 2025 to $12.5 million in 2026, even as the median decreased from $4.5 million to $3.5 million, the report found. Average 2026 revenues were $30.5 million—well above 2025’s $23.9 million and 2024’s $18 million. The share of online enterprises generating at least $2 in revenue for every dollar budgeted also has risen each year, to 43 percent in 2026. Yet, 41 percent of institutions represented anticipate an increase in program budgets while 23 percent expect a decrease.

Online learning is a “pillar” of the current higher education ecosystem, the report found, with 80 percent of chief online learning officer respondents (N=169) agreeing that leaders at their institution have made online learning a strategic direction. Administratively, the share of online enterprises housed in the provost’s office has grown, to 57 percent in fiscal 2026. Financially, online enterprises are most often funded from an institution’s general fund, at 39 percent. But just over half (51 percent) charge an online or distance education fee, typically set by a central or system administrative unit—creating what the report calls a “structural disconnect” between accountability and control.

Growth in online education is real and ongoing, the report says, “but long-term sustainability depends on how well institutions align their governance structures, financial models and program strategies with their broader institutional mission. The enterprises treating that alignment as a deliberate strategic choice now, not an afterthought to sort out once budgets stabilize, are the ones that will set the pace for the rest of the field.”

Inside Higher Ed’s 2026 Survey of Campus Chief Technology/Information Officers with Hanover Research found that 64 percent were confident in the quality of their institution’s online and hybrid course offerings, but a plurality (33 percent) described their institution’s technology support for pathways such as microcredentials, certificates and badges, in particular, as limited.

In an increasingly competitive online landscape, most CTOs indicated that their institution had adjusted its technology strategy in the last year in response: About a quarter each reported improved online course design support for faculty, upgraded student-facing technology and platforms, increased marketing and recruitment technology, enhanced student engagement and retention tools, and increased investments in alternative credential and microcredential offerings.

title: What New Research Reveals About Student Success
summary:
What New Research Reveals About Student Success
Joshua.Bay Tue, 08/18/2026 - 03:00 AM

Recent studies on subjects including mental health, financial vulnerability and career preparation challenge assumptions about what students need to succeed.

Byline(s)
Joshua Bay
full_text:
Student success is often measured through outcomes such as persistence and completion, but it is shaped by whether students have the resources and support they need to reach those milestones. Recent research captures the range of factors that can influence students’ ability to succeed, including mental health, financial vulnerability and career literacy.

The findings also highlight potential blind spots for colleges and universities seeking to boost student success, including students who may not know about available resources, populations that institutions may be undercounting and supports that may not be reaching those who need them most.

Here are four recent research findings that challenge assumptions about what students need and how institutions should respond.

Financial vulnerability and mental health are deeply connected.

Students’ mental health can influence whether they persist and ultimately complete college, and most institutions offer robust mental health supports for them. But a recent analysis from Trellis Strategies found that students experiencing financial vulnerability or basic needs insecurity are less likely than their peers to know whether their institution offers mental health or counseling services.

Researchers analyzed disparities in anxiety, depression and loneliness among college students using findings from the postsecondary research and consulting firm’s 2025 Student Financial Wellness Survey. Financially vulnerable students reported substantially higher rates of all three mental health conditions than their financially secure peers.

At the same time, 24 percent of financially vulnerable students reported not knowing whether their institution offers mental health or counseling services, compared with 17 percent of their more financially secure peers.

Morgan Beckham, research analyst at Trellis Strategies and author of the report, said the finding underscores a disconnect between students’ need for support and their awareness of the resources available to them.

“A lot of institutions are investing in mental health resources, so the issue is not necessarily that there is nothing there for them,” Beckham said. “But when you are trying to reach students that have challenges or other special circumstances that are happening, it can be difficult because they might not have as much time to go and find the resources for themselves.”

“It’s important for institutions to have that proactive outreach and make sure that they’re reaching students with those campus touch points,” she added.

Emergency aid may not be reaching students who need it.

An unexpected expense is one of the most common reasons students stop out of college. Research has shown that emergency aid—a timely grant that helps students cover unexpected costs—can greatly improve the odds that they stay enrolled and complete a degree or credential.

However, a new analysis from the Hope Center for Student Basic Needs at Temple University found that despite growth in emergency aid programs on college campuses, far fewer students are receiving that assistance.

The analysis is based on data from Trellis’s most recent Student Financial Wellness Survey of more than 65,000 undergraduates across 153 institutions nationwide. It found that the share of students receiving emergency aid fell from 44 percent in fall 2021 to 4 percent in fall 2025—a decline of roughly 90 percent.

Muhammad Kara, policy and research analyst at the center, said the decline suggests colleges are either failing to publicize available support or operating programs that are too limited in scope or funding to meet student need.

Unlike traditional financial aid, which is packaged months before a term and disbursed on a fixed schedule, he said, emergency aid is designed to help students respond quickly to an unforeseen financial crisis and can be distributed on short notice.

“These have real-world applications,” Kara said. “If a student can’t pay a medical bill or afford food or housing, they’re really not going to be focused on their academics.”

Colleges may serve far more autistic students than they realize.

As colleges work to improve student success, new research suggests they may be underestimating the size of a particular population on campus: autistic students.

A new study from Michigan State University examined 731 publications, reviewed 16 common survey instruments used at postsecondary institutions and inspected codebooks from six federal datasets to come up with the estimate that over 280,000 autistic students are currently enrolled in U.S. colleges and universities—three to five times more than previous data suggested.

Researchers said many institutions may not realize how many autistic students they serve, making it more difficult to design policies, services and supports that help them succeed.

Brad Cox, associate professor of higher, adult and lifelong education at Michigan State, said earlier estimates of autistic college enrollment relied on decades-old data, leaving researchers and policymakers with an incomplete picture of this student group.

“It’s hard to serve a population you don’t know is even there, because autism is an identity that isn’t always apparent, isn’t always visible,” Cox said. “As a result, this population, despite all of the broader public attention that has come to autism over the last decade or two, in a college environment, these students are still underreported and underrecognized.”

Career preparation is about more than job-ready skills.

Students who understand how their skills, interests and education connect to a range of career pathways may be better positioned to navigate a rapidly changing job market, according to new research from the DeBruce Foundation.

The report from the nonprofit, which focuses on expanding pathways to economic growth and opportunity, found that people with higher degrees of career literacy—the ability to understand, plan and navigate career pathways—conduct broader job searches, are more open to changing careers over time and experience greater employment security than their peers. Those skills, researchers argue, will become increasingly important as artificial intelligence continues to reshape the labor market.

According to the findings, individuals with high career literacy considered about six potential jobs during a job search, compared to roughly two among those with low career literacy. The research also found that people with both strong career literacy and robust professional networks explored 22 percent more career options outside their current path than their peers and earned an average of $40,000 more annually.

Leigh Anne Taylor Knight, executive director and chief operating officer of the DeBruce Foundation, said career literacy—in contrast to career readiness, which focuses on developing academic, technical and employability skills needed to enter the workforce—helps students understand their strengths, explore different career pathways and make informed career decisions.

“Career literacy really focuses on, ‘Hey, what do you really like to do? What do you do well?’ in order to open the student up to consider multiple careers,” Taylor Knight said. “That’s just imperative in today’s economy, and we’re only seeing AI accelerating that.”

title: Plagiarism, Even if Proven, Does Not Deserve Moral Prosecution
summary:
Plagiarism, Even if Proven, Does Not Deserve Moral Prosecution
sara.custer@in… Tue, 08/18/2026 - 03:00 AM

Jason Arday, neurodivergence and what happens when academic accountability becomes public punishment.

Byline(s)
Bankole Johnson
full_text:
Jason Arday is dead at 41.

Police have described his death as unexpected but not suspicious. We do not know its medical cause, and it would be irresponsible to turn chronology into causation. His death does not prove that public scrutiny killed him, just as it does not settle the allegations made against him. But it would be equally irresponsible to ignore the human consequences of a process in which academic questions, institutional anxiety, media appetite, race and neurodivergence became fused into a single public judgment.

Nine days before his death, Arday resigned from his professorship at the University of Cambridge after weeks of intense allegations about plagiarism, his academic biography and parts of his public life story. His family has described a prolonged campaign of abuse, harassment and misinformation. Grief does not require us to pretend that the questions surrounding his scholarship were trivial. The textual overlaps identified in his work were serious enough to demand a rigorous inquiry.

But four different matters were repeatedly collapsed into one: demonstrable similarities with another scholar’s work, an academic finding of plagiarism, a conclusion of deliberate fraud and the destruction of a person’s reputation. Those are not synonyms. The first can often be established by comparison. The second requires the application of scholarly standards. The third requires evidence about knowledge and intent. The fourth is a punishment—one that began to be imposed before the preceding questions had been finally adjudicated.

When Fact-Checking Becomes Character Prosecution

The controversy over Arday’s claim to have run 600 miles in six days illustrates the problem. Such a feat would mean averaging 100 miles a day for six consecutive days and would approach world-class ultradistance performance. Journalists were entitled to ask for records, witnesses or routes. When the account was later described as 600 miles completed over 12 days, the discrepancy was plainly a legitimate subject for correction.

Yet what did that discrepancy prove about the attribution of sentences in a doctoral thesis? Nothing directly.

At most, it was collateral evidence about the reliability of a public biography. It could justify further checking; it could not establish academic intent. Had an otherwise obscure white professor made the same extravagant claim over dinner, many colleagues would probably have smirked, remembered him as an embellisher and moved on. In Arday’s case, it became an exhibit in a national prosecution of character.

That is the point at which fact-checking becomes something else. The press began by investigating what Jason Arday had done. It ended by prosecuting what kind of person it believed him to be. Once the public was invited to see him as a fantasist, every ambiguity could be interpreted against him. A disputed athletic story contaminated the interpretation of scholarship, questions about scholarship contaminated memories of childhood and the accumulated narrative was then offered as proof of the narrative itself.

The Gifts and Vulnerabilities of Neurodivergence

Several members of my own family are on the autism spectrum. I have sometimes wondered whether elements of the same neurotype are present in me.

What I recognize is not merely a catalog of impairment. It is an ability to see with unusual clarity and to speak without the fear that ordinarily makes people soften or withhold what they perceive. Some neurodivergent minds are less governed by convention and the social choreography through which uncomfortable truths are usually concealed. That clarity without fear can be an extraordinary gift in science, medicine and scholarship.

The same mind can also be unusually vulnerable. Directness may be read as arrogance. Literalness may be mistaken for evasion. Intense concentration in one domain may coexist with disorganization in another. Autobiographical chronology, executive function, social inference and the management of institutional politics may be far less secure than abstract reasoning. Prolonged masking and the effort of appearing conventionally competent can culminate in profound exhaustion and loss of function.

None of this proves Arday’s account of any disputed event. Autism is neither an alibi nor an accusation. It does not exempt anyone from standards of accuracy or honesty. It does, however, require that questions of communication, memory, intent and support be evaluated by people who understand neurodivergence rather than by commentators who treat every inconsistency as evidence of dishonesty.

Would the Country Have Cared if He Were Not Black?

A white Cambridge professor accused of plagiarism could certainly face serious professional consequences. But would one professor’s thesis have become a national morality play about whether an entire class of people deserved entry into elite universities? I doubt it.

Arday was not treated merely as an individual scholar facing allegations. Some coverage explicitly cast him as a symbol of diversity policy. His appointment had been celebrated as evidence of progress; his alleged failures were then used as evidence that the progress itself was fraudulent. The Black scholar is made representative twice: first when his success is displayed, and again when his imperfection is weaponized.

An ordinary white academic is usually permitted to fail as an individual. A prominent Black academic can be made to fail on behalf of a race, an appointment policy and an entire philosophy of inclusion. That does not place his scholarship beyond scrutiny. It explains why scrutiny became spectacle, and why the story traveled so far beyond Cambridge.

That distinction matters. Testing an extraordinary biographical claim may be legitimate journalism. Treating every eccentricity, disputed recollection or implausible boast as corroboration of academic dishonesty is something else. It invites a seductive but unsound inference: If one claim is doubtful, perhaps the whole person is doubtful.

There was a legitimate public interest story here. There were serious questions about attribution, academic standards and Cambridge’s appointment procedures. But somewhere along the way, investigation became excavation. His running, his charity work, his childhood, his disabilities, his memories and eventually almost the entire architecture of his life were placed in the dock.

In forensic medicine and psychiatry, one learns how easily evidence changes status as it passes through institutions. No participant in that chain needs consciously to lie. Each can say that he relied upon what came before. Yet by the end, inference has hardened into fact and the human being has disappeared beneath a biography assembled from partial truths. The record no longer describes the person; it replaces him.

That is what troubles me most in the Arday case. An academic inquiry should be forensic, not theatrical. It should ask what each item of evidence proves, what it does not prove and how much uncertainty remains. It should resist the seduction of a single totalizing explanation.

Accountability Without Annihilation

Universities need a more civilized model of accountability. Allegations should be investigated promptly by genuinely independent panels working to published deadlines. Textual overlap should be distinguished from deliberate deception. The conduct of supervisors, examiners, editors and appointing institutions should be scrutinized alongside that of the accused scholar.

Where neurodivergence is plausibly relevant, real expertise should be included—not to manufacture immunity, but to assess communication, cognition and support needs accurately. Complainants and respondents of scholarly misconduct should both be protected from intimidation. Confidential psychological support should be available independently of the investigative body. Findings should be reasoned, transparent and proportionate, with correction, sanction and rehabilitation each considered on its merits.

Jason Arday’s death neither acquits nor convicts him. Death is not evidence. What it should do is restore a sense of human scale.

Mercy is not acquittal. Due process is not indulgence. Support is not a lowering of standards.

We should be able to defend the integrity of scholarship without abandoning the dignity of the scholar. We should be able to correct a record without allowing the record to replace the person.

Let us not wait for another tragic death before we learn how to support difficult brilliance while it is still alive.

title: US states accuse Meta of covering up research on teen social media addiction in pivotal trial
summary:
State attorneys general claim tech company intentionally designed addictive products that harm young people

Continue reading...
full_text:
Lawyers representing 29 US states have accused Meta of covering up internal research showing Instagram was addictive for teenagers. In a packed courtroom Tuesday, on the opening day of a landmark legal challenge, they said the company knew its products harmed children but hid that information from the public.

“I heard from many of you at jury selection that the health and wellbeing of kids is a shared responsibility,” said Megan O’Neill, a deputy attorney general for California, in her opening statements. “Meta didn’t do its share.”

O’Neill told jurors that she would be giving them a preview of what they could expect to see over the course of the trial, which would include witness testimony and internal documents the attorneys general uncovered while investigating the social media company.

She referenced one document that said, “the young ones are the best ones”, along with another where Meta stated: “Teens are hooked despite how it makes them feel. Instagram is addictive.”

“They knew,” O’Neill said. “Time and again, profits won.”

The lawsuit against Meta accuses the parent company of Instagram and Facebook of deliberately designing addictive products that lure in young people and damage their mental health.

The jury trial is taking place in federal court in Oakland, California, and is expected to last six to eight weeks. The jury will hear from Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, Instagram CEO Adam Mosseri and other company executives. After opening statements on Tuesday, the government called former employee turned whistleblower Arturo Béjar as its first witness.

The 233-page lawsuit, first filed in October 2023, alleges that Meta regularly collects data on children under the age of 13 without parental permission in violation of federal and state laws. The lawmakers claim in court documents that Meta “refuses to abandon its use of known harmful features” and that its motives are based solely on profit to “maximize its financial gains”.

The suit was filed jointly by 29 state attorneys general in what is known as multidistrict litigation, though the trial proceedings will be led by attorneys for California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey.

The sweeping legal proceedings could have profound consequences for the social media company. The attorneys general say that if Meta is found liable, damages could be as high as $200bn – an amount equivalent to the company’s 2025 annual revenue. The lawmakers are also asking that Meta be compelled to change the design of its products to make them safer for children, which may have longer-term effects than a fine.

Meta denies all allegations. In opening statements, Paul Schmidt, a lawyer for Meta, said the internal documents and emails the government lawyers showed the jury were taken out of context and cherry-picked from longer conversations. He said Meta has done several studies on young users with the goal of asking “what can we do to support teens in this space”.

Schmidt said that Meta has disabled more than 1m accounts of children under the age of 13 and that it is “acting in a meaningful way to remove” young users.

In a statement, a company spokesperson said: “Rather than sticking to the facts or the law, the states have instead decided to chase an outlandish payout.

“The state AGs may call this a landmark case, but their limited claims are unsubstantiated and their financial demands are vastly disproportionate. The AGs offer no proof anyone in their states was misled, claim benign features like having an additional Instagram account somehow harmed their residents, and attempt to penalize Meta for industry-wide challenges like age verification.”

The attorneys general disagree, saying Meta “developed and refined a set of psychologically manipulative” features designed to maximize people’s time on its apps. Those include an infinite scrolling recommendation algorithm, constant notification alerts, thumbs-up “likes” and visual filters for altering one’s image.

The lawmakers say young people are especially vulnerable to falling prey to such features and that excessive time online can lead to increased depression, anxiety, eating disorders and other mental health issues.

Mounting lawsuits

The federal trial comes just two weeks after a judge ordered Meta to pay $567m to New Mexico in a similar case brought by the state’s attorney general. This was the second court-ordered financial penalty for Meta in New Mexico, bringing the total it is responsible for paying the state to $942m. A state trial in Tennessee is also now under way

Families, school districts and other attorneys general have brought thousands of lawsuits against Meta and other social media companies in recent years. The plaintiffs hope a death-by-a-thousand-cuts legal strategy will induce Meta to change its social networks to be safer for children.

In California, thousands of coordinated cases have been filed in state court against Meta, YouTube, TikTok and Snap. Meta and YouTube lost the first of those cases to go to trial in February, being ordered to pay $6m to the young woman who brought the suit. (TikTok and Snap settled before the case went to trial.) Two more lawsuits slated to go to trial this summer, one federal and one in California state court, also settled for undisclosed sums.

The lawsuits have borrowed from the legal approach used against tobacco companies in the 1990s, which focused on cigarettes’ addictive qualities and the makers’ knowledge that their products caused harm. Those thousands of suits resulted in a $200bn payout by the four largest companies in 1998 and enforced changes to their marketing practices.

Russell Coleman, the attorney general of Kentucky, said he and his colleagues were using that blueprint and aimed to show the jury that “Meta concealed what it knew about the harm its products cause young people”.

“AGs are in the perfect position to get this done,” he added. “We did it with the tobacco settlement in the 1990s. We did it with the companies behind the opioid crisis. We’ll do it again with Meta.”

title: Meta trial begins with states accusing social media giant of exploiting, intentionally addicting children
summary: Meta Platforms rejected accusations by U.S. states that it intentionally sought to addict children to its Facebook and Instagram platforms in pursuit of profit as a trial that could reshape some of the most popular apps on the planet got underway Tuesday.
full_text:
Meta Platforms rejected accusations by U.S. states that it intentionally sought to addict children to its Facebook and Instagram platforms in pursuit of profit as a trial that that could reshape some of the most popular apps on the planet got underway Tuesday

A bipartisan group of 29 U.S. states is suing Meta, seeking potentially tens or hundreds ‌of billions of dollars in penalties and changes to how Meta does business.

Four lead states — California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey — accused Meta of designing Facebook and Instagram to hook young users, fuelling anxiety, depression and even suicide, and misleading consumers about the platforms' safety. All 29 states accused Meta of violating federal law by improperly collecting and using children's personal data.

Experts have called the trial in the Oakland, Calif., federal court, which heard opening statements Tuesday, the biggest legal test yet of social media's effects on young users. Meta and other social media companies ​including Snap, TikTok parent ByteDance and YouTube parent Alphabet face thousands of lawsuits by states, municipalities, school districts and individuals over ​whether their products harm young users.

Megan O'Neill, a deputy attorney general for California, told the eight-person jury that Meta's business model was to "hook the users, hold them for as long as they can, harvest their data, and then hide the truth from the public."

"It worked especially well for kids," O'Neill added. "Meta needed kids, and it needed to ​reassure the people who cared about those kids that the kids are safe."

Meta's lawyer Paul Schmidt said there was "no dispute" that some social media users face struggles, but ⁠that research showed no clear link between adolescents' social ⁠media use and a lack of well-being. He also said Mark Zuckerberg, Meta's co-founder and CEO, shared the company's desire ‌to improve its services, and not make them dangerous.

"They don't believe they're going to do well if people don't like their service," Schmidt said.

Judge could order changes to Instagram, Facebook

Jurors are expected to issue an advisory verdict — a non-binding position the judge could take into consideration as guidance — but U.S. District Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers will ultimately determine Meta's liability.

If she finds Meta liable, Rogers could impose civil penalties and order changes to Facebook and Instagram. Meta has said penalties could be as high as $1.4 trillion US, close to the Menlo Park, California-based company's market value.

Attorneys general said at a hearing last week the amount could be ⁠closer to $200 billion US, or about three years of after-tax profit for Meta.

California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey also want Meta to overhaul Facebook and Instagram, including by eliminating likes and the infinite scroll that encourages views of new posts, setting time limits for younger users, and enforcing restrictions to keep children under 13 offline.

First witness testifies

After opening arguments concluded, former Meta safety engineer Arturo Bejar began testifying as the states' first witness.

Bejar has long said Meta knew its child ‌safety tools did not work, and has testified against the company in four trials. Meta sought to block his testimony, allegedly for deleting Signal messages with former employees, but Rogers rejected what she considered a long-shot bid to eliminate a key witness.

Bejar told jurors that "move fast and break things" was a mantra at Meta, which he said took a "don't ask, don't tell" approach to monitoring whether children under 13 were online.

"Many products were shipped into the world," such as Reels short-form videos, "and safety was not a consideration in how it was initially deployed," Bejar said.

Employees viewed Instagram as 'drug,' states allege

Zuckerberg and Instagram chief Adam ​Mosseri are expected to testify. The trial is scheduled to last six weeks.

Meta shares traded lower most of Tuesday and closed down 4.4 per cent at $543.67 US.

O'Neill said the states were not trying to put Meta out of business, saying social media "has some benefits for some people."

But she said Meta ⁠exploited children by researching how their brains work and react to online stimuli, and by tracking their interactions on its apps.

She said an internal email sent to Mosseri noted that "teen time spent" was the goal, and that ⁠Meta employees viewed Instagram as a "drug" and themselves as "pushers."

"Meta found the younger a kid is when they start using the app, the better," O'Neill said.

Schmidt acknowledged that employees might use "loose" language in private, but ⁠said Meta's products ⁠were not addictive, and that jurors would hear what the employee who called ​Instagram a drug did to make it safer.

Critics gather outside court

Some critics of Meta spoke outside the courthouse as the trial began.

Among them was Mary Rodee, who said her 15-year-old son Riley Basford died by suicide in 2021 after being victimized ​by a predator on Facebook.

"They call it spontaneous suicide," she ⁠said. "I call it what it was, the predictable outcome of a system that protects corporations instead of children."

The lawsuit began in 2023, two years after whistleblower Frances Haugen told a U.S. Senate committee that Meta knew its products were unsafe for children and knew how to make them safe, but did nothing in order to pursue higher profits. In March, a Los Angeles jury ordered Meta and Google to pay $6 million US to a 20-year-old woman who said she became addicted to Instagram and YouTube as a child.

Earlier this month, a New Mexico judge ordered Meta to pay $567 million US to address teenagers' mental health after that state's attorney general called its platforms a public nuisance.

Tennessee's attorney general is also suing ⁠Meta, raising similar claims about Instagram. That case is on trial ‌in Nashville.

title: Why is PM CARES Fund keeping large sums idle, asks RTI activist
summary: PM CARES Fund, a public charitable trust established in March 2020 to support relief efforts during public health emergencies and other disasters, is chaired by the Prime Minister and funded entirely through voluntary contributions
full_text:
The PM CARES (Prime Minister’s Citizen Assistance and Relief in Emergency Situations) Fund received donations of ₹480 crore in 2024-25, down about 30% over the previous year, according to audited financial statements for 2023-24 and 2024-25 made available on Tuesday (August 18, 2026). Its total income, however, grew to ₹1,279.9 crore, up 41% over the previous year. The documents were released after a failure to upload annual disclosures since FY 2022-23.

The Hindu had highlighted the lapse on August 8.

The PM CARES Fund, a public charitable trust established in March 2020 to support relief efforts during public health emergencies and other disasters, is chaired by the Prime Minister and funded entirely through voluntary contributions, according to information released by the Union government.

Limited spending

Reacting to the belated disclosure, Anjali Bhardwaj, co-convenor of the National Campaign for People’s Right to Information (NCPRI), said in a social media post: “Finally the audit statement of PMCARES Fund for 2024-25 has been made public! Key highlights — utilised only 0.01% of available ₹8,452 crore!”.

Ms. Bhardwaj was referring to the fact that, while the fund received a total of ₹1,279.9 crore in FY 2024-25 from net donations, interest on bank and fixed deposits, and refunds from implementing agencies, it spent only ₹87.85 lakh, which is 0.01% of the fund’s closing balance.

From March 2020 to March 31, 2025, the fund has spent less than one-fifth (18.4%) of its total income.

Opaque filings

The closing balance of PM CARES Fund stood at ₹8,452.06 crore in FY 2024-25, 17.8% higher than at the end of the previous year.

“Why is the PM CARES Fund keeping such large sums of money idle,” Ms. Bhardwaj asked. She also noted that while ₹324 crore had been refunded by implementing agencies in 2024-25, no information was provided on the nature of these payments, reasons for the refunds, or the identity of the agencies involved.

“Were refunds done to evade accountability for faulty equipment,” she said. “Also why have accompanying notes to the audit report not been uploaded?”

Lack of accountability

Ms. Bhardwaj said a fund set up to help citizens during disasters, which has accumulated thousands of crores including from foreign sources, is “shrouded in secrecy”.

“Still no information available on sources of funds,” she said. “The PM CARES Fund continues to evade public scrutiny by refusing to submit itself to the RTI Act”.

The PM CARES Fund, established three days before the close of the FY 2019-20, has faced scrutiny over its transparency, following the absence of public audit statements after FY 2022-23. Critics have questioned why a fund — which accepts public money, including Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) contributions from public sector undertakings and donations from government employees — is made to seem like a public authority.

The Prime Minister chairs the fund in his ex officio capacity and Union Cabinet Ministers are its trustees.

title: European universities belong in every admissions conversation. Most advisors don’t know that
summary:
As English-taught options to top-ranking universities expand in Europe, Dr. Melissa Morrison argues advisors must treat Europe as a top-tier destination – and the advice around it must catch up.

The post European universities belong in every admissions conversation. Most advisors don’t know that appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
When I was applying to university, I assumed I would stay close to home. I grew up near Washington, D.C., where college, for most of the people I knew, was a four-year extension of high school.

Then a trip to Europe in my senior year changed my plan in a way I was not prepared for.

I can’t quite name the single moment that did it. Maybe it was the sound of a tram in Vienna, maybe it was a café where the waitress answered in the language I had practiced only in classrooms, maybe it was noticing that my peers were traveling between countries, as if it were the most ordinary thing in the world. I came home unable to picture my life in one place.

The irony is that the path that rerouted my life – a solo flight to Europe, a degree from a US-Swiss dual-accredited university in southern Switzerland, speaking the languages I had practiced only in classrooms – was a path nobody at my high school was capable of advising me on, and yet was the path that spoke to me long before I boarded the flight.

The European admissions landscape is changing

The same kind of move I made to Europe is now being made by more students across the globe.

More than 8,000 fully English-taught degree programmes are now in Europe. That’s more than a tenfold increase from the 725 that existed in 2001.

The number of international students at German universities has nearly doubled in a decade. What once felt niche or inaccessible has now become visible, ambitious, and increasingly mainstream.

The new generation is a global one

The applicant considering Europe today is more comparative, more outcome-focused, and less likely to be persuaded by destination branding alone. They want to know where they can study and where they can build a future.

That includes questions about employability, cost of living, qualification recognition, and how different systems support life after graduation.

The applicant considering Europe today is more comparative, more outcome-focused, and less likely to be persuaded by destination branding alone

That shift shows up most clearly at the most selective institutions. For families whose default has long been the Ivy League and Oxbridge, Bocconi for economics, TU Delft for engineering, and Sciences Po for social sciences now appear on the same shortlist.

Europe is no longer viewed simply as an alternative. For many of the highest-ambition applicants we work with, it is part of that conversation from the first session.

Better access does not eliminate complexity

The challenge is that more English-taught options do not automatically make Europe easier to navigate. Students may see a region; advisors need to explain the differences underneath it. That means understanding how academic structures vary across countries and how professional pathways differ.

Advisors must match Europe’s new ambition

If Europe’s fully English-taught degrees are reshaping the admissions conversation, advising must respond at the same level. Students need help getting into top programs in Europe. This means that they need an expert who can advise accordingly.

That is the work the next generation of advisors needs to be ready for. The region has changed.

Advising must, too.

About the author: Dr. Melissa Morrison heads Europe, Canada and Australia admissions at Crimson Education, where she oversees a large-scale international admissions portfolio supporting more than 1,000 applicants each year across multiple destination markets.

With more than a decade of experience in admissions and student strategy, her work brings together strategic oversight, operational leadership and a deep understanding of how students navigate complex cross-border admissions systems.

She holds a degree from Franklin University in Switzerland, a Masters degree in School Psychology from Temple University, and a PhD in Organizational Psychology from Liberty University. In addition to her work in admissions, Melissa has published research in peer-reviewed medical journals and presented at more than 50 international conferences.

title: 25 Effective Instructional Strategies For Educators
summary:
Engage, assess and motivate students with these 25 easy-to-use instructional strategies for any discipline

The post 25 Effective Instructional Strategies For Educators appeared first on Top Hat.
full_text:
Instructional strategies refer to the techniques instructors use to deliver their lessons. Effective instructional strategies—also known as teaching strategies—help students become actively involved in the learning process. When done right, instructional strategies also support students in reaching their learning objectives.

By reading the guide below (or downloading this free list of instructional strategies), you’ll gain a solid understanding of the various types of teaching strategies, why they’re important and how they can be applied to the learning process to benefit both professors and students.

In this guide, you’ll:

Learn what instructional strategies are and the various strategies educators can use to teach more effectively

Gain a deeper understanding of how instructional strategies for teachers—including formal and informal assessments, case studies, debates, flipped classrooms and more—play into the overall student learning experience

Get equipped to implement instructional strategies that are appropriate for your course in order to become more effective at teaching and engaging students

Get access to a free instructional strategies list, packed with 25 easy-to-implement exercises for your next course

With this collection of teaching strategies, you’ll be ready to guide students towards success in any classroom setting. Plus, putting a few of these techniques into practice will ensure students come to class prepared to engage with the material, with their peers and with you.

1. What are instructional strategies?

Instructional strategies encompass any type of learning technique a teacher uses to help students learn or gain a better understanding of the course material. They allow teachers to make the learning experience more fun and practical, and can also include explicit teaching when instructors need clear, direct guidance for a skill or concept, while encouraging students to take more of an active role in their education. The objective of using instructional strategies beyond subject comprehension is to create students who are independent, strategic learners. The hope is, with time and practice, students will be able to select the right strategies on their own and use them effectively to complete tasks.

There are various instructional strategies examples that can be used effectively at all levels and in subject areas, with a wide range of learning styles and diverse learning needs. These learning strategies motivate students by improving their engagement, capturing their attention and encouraging them to focus on not only remembering course material, but truly understanding it, while supporting different types of learners in unique ways.

Educators who use instructional strategies allow students to make meaningful connections between concepts learned in class and real-life situations, helping them apply concepts beyond school. They offer an opportunity for students to demonstrate their knowledge and course correct on their own when needed. Teachers also benefit from using instructional strategies because they’re able to better monitor and assess student performance through different methods of evaluation.

2. What’s the difference between instructional strategies, teaching strategies, teaching techniques and teaching practices?

In the dynamic landscape of higher education, understanding the nuances between instructional strategies, teaching strategies, teaching techniques, and teaching practices is crucial for educators aiming to enhance their pedagogical approach. Instructional strategies encompass a broader framework, outlining the overarching plans and methods employed to facilitate learning. These strategies guide the selection of teaching methods and techniques, serving as the foundation for effective educational practices. On the other hand, teaching strategies delve into the specific approaches instructors use to convey information and engage students. These strategies act as the vehicles through which instructional goals are achieved, embracing diverse methodologies such as collaborative learning, active participation, and technology integration.

Zooming in further, teaching techniques are the tactical tools and methods employed within a specific teaching strategy. These are the hands-on practices educators implement to deliver content, foster understanding, and promote critical thinking. Examples include case studies, role-playing, and interactive discussions. Finally, teaching practices encompass the comprehensive application of instructional, teaching, and technical strategies in the classroom. It reflects the amalgamation of various methods tailored to the unique needs of learners and the subject matter. By dissecting these components, higher education professors can refine their pedagogical repertoire, fostering a rich and dynamic learning environment for their students.

3. Types of instructional or teaching strategies

There are far too many types of instructional or teaching strategies to catalog in one place. And there’s no single, specific way to group them together. While the categories below are by no means exhaustive, instructional strategies often fall under general groupings. These include: active learning, assessment-based, group-based, advanced strategies, organizational (or classroom management) and tiered.

4. Active learning instructional strategies and teaching strategy examples

4.1. Exit tickets

Before students leave your learning environment, ask them to answer a question related to a key concept discussed in the lesson that day. They can write it down on a piece of paper or index card. Questions can be simple, like asking students what they found most interesting about the lesson. Or, they can be more complex, such as having them draw a sketch that demonstrates what they learned, or asking them to connect the key concept they learned to a real-life situation. Have students hand the ‘tickets‘ to you as they exit (or have them submit a response to your discussion board), then review the responses.

The feedback can help educators determine which students need additional teaching in specific areas. Using this approach, teachers gain a quick understanding of how the whole class is grasping and reacting to the material.

Use the information from the exit tickets to form groups in the class that follows. Place students at similar levels of understanding, or who have similar views on a topic, together. Conversely, group students with opposing views together in order to foster debate and conversation. Learn more about the types of exit tickets you can use in your next course—download an exit ticket template here.

4.2. Flipped classrooms

Regardless of where you teach, flipping your classroom is one of the most popular forms of active learning and among the most well-known instructional strategies. As a form of blended learning, it combines online learning with face-to-face instruction. Instead of using classroom time for lecturing, educators provide students with a pre-recorded lecture to watch prior to class. They’re often concise, posted to sites like YouTube, or presented in the form of a podcast that students can listen to at home or during their commute, where students spend pre-class time on videos or audio before meeting in person. Educators can then use classroom time to engage students in learning activities related to the lecture they’ve already seen or heard.

Flipped classrooms are an effective teaching technique because they allow students to review and learn concepts at their own pace. Students are then free to complete more interactive and collaborative work in class, including discussions and tasks with their peers and teacher. They can also collaborate and discuss material through online forums with peers and subject matter experts. In class, students can actively apply concepts via peer learning, group work, and presentations.

Flipped learning helps keep students continuously engaged in class instead of just passively listening. And it makes good use of downtime by allowing students to combine a workout or commute time with further learning, when it’s most convenient for them. Built to enable this strategy, Top Hat makes it simple to adopt a flipped classroom—simply run quizzes prior to your lecture and create interactive discussions for students to collaborate during class time.
